strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation with clear identification of LDM-based AiOR limitations and useful scale-space analysis insights
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 5 restoration tasks, multiple benchmarks, thorough ablation studies, and generalization testing
Strong empirical results achieving state-of-the-art generative AiOR performance with significant 10× inference speedup
Sound technical approach with well-justified architectural modifications (cross-attention for conditioning, LRT for detail preservation)
Excellent visual results with good fine-detail preservation and demonstrated generalization to real-world degradations
Good implementation details and reproducibility documentation with clear training/inference specifications
weaknesses: Limited fundamental novelty - primarily an application of existing VAR method to AiOR domain rather than introducing new concepts
Incremental architectural contributions with cross-attention being standard practice and LRT design appearing somewhat ad-hoc without strong theoretical justification
Scale-space analysis in Section 3.2 relies heavily on qualitative visual examples rather than rigorous quantitative analysis
Generalization claims overstated - testing on 'unseen' degradations still within same dataset distributions; true out-of-distribution generalization not demonstrated

strengths: Strong empirical results across multiple image restoration tasks with 10× faster inference than LDM-based methods, demonstrating clear practical value
Comprehensive and well-designed experimental evaluation including comparisons with generative and non-generative methods, extensive ablations, and user study validation
Insightful scale-space analysis revealing that VAR naturally captures degradations at coarse scales and scene details at fine scales, providing useful understanding of the approach
Well-motivated technical approach appropriately adapting VAR for AioR with clear justification for why VAR outperforms LDMs (avoiding iterative denoising), establishing a new effective paradigm
Excellent generalization capabilities demonstrated on unseen degradations, mixed degradations, and real-world scenarios, showing robustness beyond training distribution
Clear presentation with effective visualizations and well-structured methodology that makes the paper accessible and reproducible in spirit
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty—primarily combines existing techniques (VAR, cross-attention, VAE fine-tuning) with the LRT being a relatively simple component; incremental technical contribution overall
Baseline comparison fairness concerns: publicly released LDM checkpoints may be suboptimally configured for AioR; unclear if PromptIR and AWRaCLe were fairly compared or underperformed

Insufficient design justification for key choices: why LRT outperforms alternatives (limited HART comparison), why VAE decoder fine-tuning is necessary (no ablation), RoPE resolution scaling rationale
Scale-space analysis in Section 3.2, while interesting, lacks rigor and theoretical depth; missing connections to classical multi-scale processing literature

Incomplete computational analysis: wall-clock timing comparisons with baselines on identical hardware missing; O(log n) vs O(n log n) claims are standard knowledge without comprehensive practical validation
Scalability limitations unaddressed: no high-resolution experiments (2K/4K); unclear if 256×256 RoPE scaling limits maximum resolution; practical applicability to modern high-res scenarios unknown
Limited failure case analysis: no discussion of challenging degradation types or edge cases; all results show success cases; no characterization of when RestoreVAR may underperform
Reproducibility concerns: code availability not mentioned; user study relatively small (38 responses) without inter-rater agreement statistics; some hyperparameter details only in supplementary
Theoretical understanding limited: empirical success demonstrated but underlying principles (why VAR's prediction strategy specifically benefits restoration) not rigorously justified

strengths: Strong empirical results with ~10× speedup over LDM-based methods and consistent improvements across multiple restoration tasks (RESIZE, Snow100k, Rain13K, LOL-v1, GoP)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation including multiple metrics (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, MUSIQ, CLIPIQA), extensive ablations, user studies, and generalization testing on unseen/mixed degradations
Insightful scale-space analysis showing coarse VAR scales capture degradations while fine scales preserve scene-level details, providing useful understanding of VAR's suitability for restoration
Well-engineered technical solution combining cross-attention conditioning, latent refinement transformer, and architectural choices (RoPE embeddings, PatchGAN discriminator) in a coherent framework
Demonstrates strong generalization performance on unseen and mixed degradation datasets compared to baseline methods
Detailed supplementary materials with 15 appendix sections covering architectural details, theoretical analysis, additional ablations, and qualitative results supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: primarily engineers existing components (VAR, cross-attention, latent refinement) for a new task rather than proposing fundamentally new methods; each component is a straightforward adaptation of existing techniques

Unfair baseline comparisons: FixWizard evaluated without structure correction module; AutoDIR's evaluation setup doesn't reflect intended use; limited VAR baselines despite claims of advantage; some recent strong methods missing

Overclaimed contributions: cross-attention for image conditioning is standard practice in image-to-image translation; LRT claimed as critical but shows only marginal quantitative improvements (~0.06dB PSNR gains) despite added complexity; novelty of being first VAR-based AiOR is somewhat vacuous

Efficiency claims need clarification: 10× speedup inherently comes from VAR's architecture (autoregressive vs. iterative diffusion) rather than RestoreVAR-specific contributions; missing detailed runtime breakdown and comparison with accelerated LDM variants

Generalization claims are relative: while better than baselines, performance still degrades significantly on unseen/mixed degradations; Table 2 shows clear performance gaps across unseen degradation types; improvements sometimes marginal compared to non-generative methods

Insufficient analysis of failure cases and limitations: acknowledged poor performance on very severe degradations and extremely low-light scenarios (Fig 25, SID) but provides minimal investigation of failure modes or mitigation strategies

Latent Refinement Transformer justification unclear: Fig 14 shows LRT cannot reconstruct without VAR transformer, suggesting limited independence; unclear why discrete latent refinement is specifically needed for VAR vs. other approaches
User study has limited statistical power: only 36 responses across 50 image selections with error margins suggesting weak significance; no participant expertise/demographics provided
Scale-space analysis is descriptive rather than prescriptive: shows VAR exhibits the property but does not prove RestoreVAR design optimally exploits it or guide specific architectural choices

Presentation issues: 27-page paper with 15 appendix sections dilutes focus; dense sections difficult to follow; cross-attention design choices and loss weight selection appear ad-hoc without principled justification

strengths: Novel scale-space decomposition analysis providing genuine insight into why VAR is well-suited for image restoration, with rigorous theoretical complexity comparison showing O(n⁴) for VAR vs O(n³ log n) for diffusion

Exceptionally comprehensive experimental evaluation across 5 restoration tasks on 10+ datasets with systematic ablations validating each component, user study with rigorous statistical testing, and generalization experiments on unseen/mixed degradations
Significant practical impact: 10× faster inference than LDM-based methods while achieving state-of-the-art quality, addressing real deployment needs

Well-motivated architectural contributions specifically designed for AioR including cross-attention conditioning for semantic guidance and latent refinement transformer for handling VAE quantization artifacts
Strong empirical results demonstrating consistent improvements over both generative and non-generative baselines, with particularly impressive performance on real-world and mixed degradations
Excellent reproducibility support with detailed specifications, computational breakdowns, and promised code release
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty in individual components: cross-attention conditioning and refinement networks are well-established techniques; core contribution reduces to applying existing VAR model to AioR

Incomplete justification for fundamental advantages: while scale-space analysis is insightful, the paper doesn't deeply explain why discrete latent tokens fundamentally outperform continuous latents, or provide theoretical grounding for VAR's superiority

Experimental methodology concerns including modification of AutoDIR baseline (removal of structure correction module) without clear justification, and modest improvements over some LDM baselines in Table 1

Acknowledged but underexplored limitations: acknowledged failure on severe degradations (Figure 25, Section J) relegated to supplementary, with no clear guidance on when RestoreVAR should/shouldn't be applied

Generalization claims lack nuance: Table 2 shows variable performance across degradation types; improvements on out-of-distribution data are sometimes marginal (<5%), with insufficient analysis of which degradations generalize better
Missing comparisons with recent LDM acceleration methods (consistency models, consistency training) and limited discussion of alternative speed-up techniques
Independent training of components without exploration of joint training or fine-tuning, raising questions about whether improvements could be attributed to LDM baseline suboptimality
